title: Danielle Smith’s hold over UCP takes centre stage as 7,000 members registered for annual meeting
summary: Alberta's United Conservatives kick off their fifth annual general meeting under Premier Danielle Smith Friday, a gathering expected to reveal much about the party’s future a little more than a month…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks to party faithful at a prior United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary in 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary

Alberta's United Conservatives kick off their fifth annual general meeting under Premier Danielle Smith Friday, a gathering expected to reveal much about the party’s future a little more than a month after a divisive referendum.
Annual gathering to draw party faithful (and those in crisis of faith)
In the days after the vote, Smith said the UCP would not be turned into a vehicle for independence.
But party unity remains elusive.
Several constituency association presidents have refused to sign pledges backing the results, meaning the independence issue remains a live one heading into the weekend.
Smith herself has advocated for conservatives to band together, suggesting she expects a “really robust [and] fun” debate at the annual meeting.

“We sadly always seem to try to find the things that blow us apart. I keep on wanting to try to find the things that will draw us together,” Smith told longtime separatist Cory Morgan in a recent interview.
Some attendees, though, expect these fissures to come into public view on the convention floor over the course of the weekend.
“I think she’s going to get absolutely surprised at the AGM,” said Martin Belanger, a social media influencer who has been a vocal proponent for Alberta independence on his channel, Martyupnorth.

“If people think that Jeff Rath getting up in front of the mic last year and saying, ‘Who here is pro-independence?’ [was notable] … You’re going to get a moment like that, after moment, after moment.”

Jeffrey Rath, co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, speaks at a referendum watch party in October. At last year’s AGM, Rath received a standing ovation at a microphone after challenging Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)
For Belanger and others in his camp, frustration lies with Smith’s approach to Ottawa.
“Some people are fed up with negotiations,” Belanger said.

“In this big tent, we have different paths, and she’s trying to shove us down one path. I don’t think she’s genuine when she says she wants that discussion, because some of her actions of late don’t reflect that.”
Remarks expected from 3 conservative premiers
More than 7,000 members have registered for the event at Calgary’s BMO Centre. On Friday, candidates for the UCP board will deliver speeches.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson are expected to deliver remarks later in the day.

British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson looks on during the swearing-in ceremony at Government House in Victoria on Nov. 20. Doerkson and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe are expected to deliver remarks on Friday at the 2026 United Conservative Party annual general meeting. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
During the event, members will vote for eight people to join the party’s board while also voting on proposed policy matters. Smith will deliver a keynote address Saturday morning.

It will be a balancing act for Smith as she is tasked with appearing as though she has a reasonably united party behind her, without conceding too much ground to the separatists in the party, said Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary.

“I would imagine that there’s a substantial number of party members who are sympathetic to the idea that they have to set aside their differences, because this is the last convention going into an election,” Young said.
“What proportion of the members those are … it’s anyone’s guess, really.”
Resolutions on land acknowledgements, washrooms
Members will also vote on a series of grassroots policy resolutions during the meeting. While non-binding, they signal the desires of party faithful and have influenced party legislation in the past.
For instance, at last year’s annual general meeting, Smith pointed to recent legislation that she said was inspired by the “attack” on psychologist and media personality Jordan Peterson.
“That came from you. That was your policy last AGM. We're calling it the 'Peterson law,’” Smith said during her speech to delegates.
As she has at AGMs past, Smith will hold an “accountability session” in front of members on Saturday.
Delegates cast their votes at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary on Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
This year, delegates will debate policy resolutions that will be voted on by members during the convention, including:

items: Ending the use of land acknowledgements by the government, as well as all publicly-funded institutions and entities.
Adopting policy that would “protect the safety and privacy of women and girls in schools and public facilities,” including washrooms and change areas.
Mandate that Alberta use "all available legal avenues” to challenge federal land claims, including Indigenous claims that "may infringe on private property owners and their rights."
Pass legislation that would require an MLA who departs their party to sit as an independent member and seek a renewed mandate from voters before joining another party.

blocks.text: Notably, there are no policy resolutions tied to the notion of separating from Canada to be debated.

Near the site of the convention, some people opposed to the UCP government's priorities have promised to hold a sort of “accountability” session of their own, saying there will be “costumes, signs, music” and other forms of protest.
“There are so many awful issues!” the Calgary Raging Grannies wrote in a post on Facebook.
Who will sit on the party's board?
To many, the biggest thing to watch over the weekend will be the results of the board elections. Half of the provincial board is elected each year, with winners going on to serve two years.

Going into the next election, this group will set the rules and the processes for nomination and platform development, making this key to the party’s future, said Colin Aitchison, managing director of western Canada with Enterprise Canada.

“I think a lot of the party membership … they want the party to be best positioned to beat the NDP and Naheed Nenshi in the next election,” said Aitchison, who was a former spokesperson for the UCP under ministers Adriana LaGrange and Nicholas Milliken.
“In order to do that, you need to have a unified leadership at the top, and one that supports the current leader and their agenda.”

items: The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention

blocks.text: Some running for the party board have dismissed the idea that the disagreements that have emerged over past months can be resolved simply by supporting a unity principle.
“A strong leader should welcome a board willing to speak candidly on behalf of its members,” wrote Vince Byfield, a board candidate, on his Substack.

“Sometimes that means offering support, sometimes it means proposing alternatives, and sometimes it means saying that members have serious concerns about a particular decision. None of those actions is inherently disloyal.”
Board election results are expected to be delivered on Saturday evening, just before the adjournment of the annual general meeting.
